accepted.match: "productive efficiency" defined differently in choice and perfect-competition
accepted.reason: Reviewed: compatible at different depths. Choice mentions productive efficiency in passing (producing without waste on the PPF); Perfect Competition (owner) gives the full definition (production at minimum average total cost in long-run equilibrium). Same concept, brief vs full.

accepted.match: "deadweight loss" defined differently in monopoly and tariffs
accepted.reason: Reviewed: the same concept applied in two contexts — the lost mutually-beneficial surplus from output below the efficient level (monopoly restricting output; a tariff shrinking trade). Consistent definition, different application.

accepted.match: "barrier to entry" defined differently in monopoly and oligopoly
accepted.reason: Reviewed: compatible. Both define a barrier to entry as an obstacle that keeps new firms out; Monopoly lists the barrier types in full, Oligopoly references them as the reason only a few firms compete. Same meaning.

accepted.match: "market failure" defined differently in externalities and public-goods
accepted.reason: Reviewed: compatible. Both use 'market failure' for a situation where a free market allocates resources inefficiently; Externalities and Public Goods are two distinct SOURCES of it (third-party costs/benefits vs non-rival/non-excludable goods). Same umbrella term, different instance.

accepted.match: "federal funds rate" defined differently in monetary-policy and interest-rates
accepted.reason: Reviewed: compatible. Monetary Policy (owner) defines the federal funds rate as the Fed's policy target/tool; Interest Rates references it as the benchmark short-term rate that anchors other rates. Same rate, two lenses.
